sm: The Williamson County Board of Education meeting of November sixteenth, 2026 opens with twelve members present and no public comment. The board approves the agenda and the consent agenda by voice vote. The consent agenda included October minutes, two policies on first and final reading, field trip fees, a lease request at Hunters Bend Elementary, and several easement and right of way requests. Superintendent Dr. Webb thanks the Fairview cluster schools and Renaissance High School for the student showcase and praises the community in Fairview. He then announces that the state's T-VAAS results rated the district a level five for growth, the top score.

Dr. Webb says a state scatter plot shows Williamson County Schools as the highest achieving and highest growing district in Tennessee on the ACT, far from any other district. He also reports that the Gallup employee engagement survey improved for the fifth straight year, with the district in the ninety-first percentile and an overall score of 4.19 out of five. The culture of inclusion category improved most. Corey Mason then reads student spotlights, including a national champion in horse evaluation from Page High School, a seventh straight state cross country title for Brentwood girls, a Franklin volleyball state title, and state wins for several cheer and dance teams.

Mason continues with the Franklin band's ninth Governor's Cup, several students with perfect ACT scores, and two staff awards, for Page High's athletic director and an Oak Ridge Middle teacher. Dr. Webb closes with the district's vision statement. The board chair thanks participants in last week's community feedback sessions and announces a special called meeting on December seventh to vote on the superintendent leadership profile. Applications for superintendent open December eighth and stay open through January fourth. The board then takes up the 2027-28 calendar and the framework of the 2028-29 calendar, which includes teachers returning a day early for a new school information system replacing Skyward.

Dr. Webb explains that late starts and early releases for 2028-29 will be studied, possibly aligning them district-wide. The board approves both calendars twelve to zero. Next is the five-year capital improvement plan, a tentative schedule reviewed annually, with individual funding votes and county commission approval still required. A member moves to approve, and Mr. Bostick moves to amend it to move the Fairview Elementary replacement, at fifty-five million dollars total, into this year's intent-to-fund list. He notes Fairview is the district's oldest school, built in 1962. Dr. Padgett seconds, and other members speak about growth balance and ask how funding would work.

Staff clarify that moving Fairview up would put two and a half million dollars in this year, with thirty million shifting to the following year, and that the commission decides between bonds and impact fees. Fairview Elementary has 407 students and a capacity of 660, so impact fees could not be used until enrollment nears capacity. Staff say the commission has typically provided ten to fifteen million dollars a year for the capital plan. Mr. Bostick argues that growth is increasing in Fairview, the most affordable area of the county.

Mr. Bostick says the issue is disparity and a deteriorating building, and invites members and commissioners to tour Fairview schools. Dr. Allen says he wants to see comparable spreadsheets before voting and moves to amend, pushing the item to the December seventh special meeting. Ms. Calcote seconds, and that amendment passes eleven to one. Confusion follows about whether a second vote is needed on the main motion as amended, and one member says she voted no thinking it was a vote to table. The chair and a board attorney work through the procedure.

The board clarifies that the vote is on the original motion as amended, meaning a vote to table the capital plan to December seventh. The motion to table passes twelve to zero. The board then moves to budget items. It approves a special schools transportation reimbursement of thirty-seven thousand fifty-five dollars, twelve to zero. It also approves a public school security grant of five hundred eighty-three thousand five hundred thirty-three dollars, made up of a new state grant of four hundred twenty-five thousand nine hundred seventy-three dollars and a carryover of one hundred fifty-seven thousand five hundred sixty dollars. The vote is again twelve to zero. The next item is an intercategory salary transfer of twelve million six hundred twelve thousand four hundred fifty-five dollars.

Dr. Webb explains the salary transfer covers raises of four percent on professional pay charts, five percent on classified charts and two percent for others, moved from one budget line to proper accounts. It passes twelve to zero. The board approves five million three hundred ninety-one thousand dollars in additional medical expenses, paid from fund balance, which would leave about seventeen point nine million against an eighteen million requirement. It approves an energy tax credit of ten million eight hundred sixty-four thousand one hundred thirty-seven dollars from geothermal projects, and medical expense transfers of one hundred fifty-six thousand dollars for the cafeteria fund and sixty-three thousand dollars for the extended school program. All pass twelve to zero, and the meeting adjourns.
